listening.title: A normal Tuesday

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: Priya, you look tired. Are you sleeping badly these days?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: A bit. I'm working on a new project, so I start at seven now. My whole routine is different.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: Seven in the morning? I usually start at nine. I need two coffees before I can speak.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: I get up at five thirty, get ready fast, and take the early train. It's quiet, actually. I like it.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: And what time do you finish?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Around four. Then I go to the gym, or I catch up with a friend. It's not bad.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: My evenings are the opposite. I finish late, so I wind down at eleven and fall asleep at midnight.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That's why you're always tired! Anyway, it's temporary for me. The project ends in March.

script.speaker: Sam
script.text: Lucky you. Once in a while I'd like an early start too. But not every day.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Ask me again in March. I'm sure I'll be complaining about something else.

reading.title: Why mornings are hard
reading.text:
Most people say they are not morning people. But our mornings are not only about our bodies; they are also about the people around us.

In one study, researchers asked office workers to write down every morning task: finding keys, making coffee, checking messages, deciding what to wear. The list was longer than anyone expected. Each small task seems easy, but together they fill the first hour of the day. People who prepare these things the night before arrive at work calmer and start faster.

Another reason is social. If your partner leaves at six, you wake up at six, even if you could sleep longer. Families create routines without noticing. Children who see their parents rush every morning often become adults who rush as well.

The good news is that routines can change. Small changes work best: put your keys in the same place, make lunch the night before, and leave your phone in another room for the first twenty minutes of the day. None of these ideas is exciting, but together they make the morning feel shorter and quieter.

writing.task: Write a short email to a friend in another city describing your typical day. Include: what time you start, how you travel, one thing you enjoy, and one thing you would like to change. 60–90 words.
checklist: Use present simple for your normal routine
Use one present continuous sentence about a temporary situation
End with a question for your friend
writing.model:
Hi Karim,

How are you? Life here is busy but OK. I usually get up at seven and start work at nine. My commute takes about thirty minutes by metro, which is not too bad. In the evening I wind down with a podcast or a short walk.

At the moment I'm working on a new project, so I'm starting earlier than usual. I like the quiet mornings, but I'd like to finish before six.

What about you? Has your routine changed?

Take care,
Mohamed
